Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
229 PM EDT Mon Sep 21 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
A solid line of thunderstorms has developed from near Canaan
Valley south to Greenbrier County in West Virginia as of 2 PM.
This line is expected to move east and weaken while crossing the
mountains this afternoon. Meanwhile, have expanded the Small
Craft Advisory to include all zones starting at 6 PM tonight.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Cloudy, damp, and cool through at least mid week.

- 2) Dry conditions return later this week and into the weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Cloudy, damp, and cool through at least mid week.

A line of thunderstorms crossing the Appalachians will run out
of SBCAPE shortly, but will have some elevated (MUCAPE)
instability to work with as it progresses down the I-64
corridor. This will be enough for some downpours and lightning,
with any gusty wind potential likely limited to 45 mph or less
at the higher elevations. Some repeat thunderstorm activity is
possible where instability lingers near the mountains into
tonight which could result in an isolated flood threat.
Confidence was too low for a watch as of mid afternoon, but will
monitor as the evening progresses.

Otherwise, high pressure already in place to our north across 
southern Quebec will rapidly strengthen to near 1040 hPa by 
Tuesday night. As this occurs, northeasterly flow will 
strengthen and the CAD wedge in place to the east of the 
Appalachians will strengthen. Large scale forcing for ascent 
will also gradually increase from west to east tonight into 
Tuesday as a shortwave trough and embedded upper low approach 
from the Ohio Valley. As large scale forcing for ascent 
increases, the coverage of showers will increase substantially 
through tonight, and likely persist at times through Wednesday 
morning. The precipitation may even resemble more of a 
continuous stratiform rain shield as opposed to showers as the
CAD strengthens by later tonight.

The flow pattern across the CONUS over the next couple days will
be extremely complex, with a split flow pattern and a closed 
upper-level ridge building to the north of the upper low over 
the Ohio Valley. So while the big picture of the forecast 
tonight through Wednesday has high confidence (low clouds, cool,
and rainy), there is still some forecast uncertainty regarding 
the finer scale details. A few model solutions attempt to 
produce several inches of rainfall over localized areas as we 
become positioned in the right entrance region of a strong jet 
streak developing off to our north and east, but there is lots 
of model to model inconsistency as to if that will occur and 
where. As of now, the most likely scenario appears to be for 
most of the region to receive 1-2 inches of rainfall spread out 
over a prolonged period time tonight through Wednesday morning.
If this were to occur, the rainfall would be beneficial in 
nature given the ongoing drought conditions. However, if the 
solutions that produce isolated totals of 3-6 inches were to 
play out, there could be localized issues with flooding. Even if
the solution with higher end totals plays out, instantaneous 
rainfall rates won't be overly high given the lack of 
instability, so it would be more of a prolonged soaking rainfall
leading to areal flooding, as opposed to thunderstorms 
producing flash flooding. We'll continue to monitor this 
potential as we move forward.

Either way, Tuesday and Wednesday will feature low clouds, 
gusty northeasterly winds, and well below normal temperatures. 
Temperatures likely hold in the 60s on Tuesday, and may even 
struggle to get out of the 50s on Wednesday as the CAD wedge 
reaches its peak strength.

By Thursday, high pressure to the north nudges southward enough
to push drier air into the region and shunt most rain chances
south into the Carolinas. Cloud breaks likely develop, though
temperatures remain below normal.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions return later this week and into
the weekend.

Surface high pressure builds northwest of the forecast area 
beginning on Friday as a surface low pressure tracks northward off 
the East Coast. Primarily dry conditions are expected, although
a nearby low pressure system brings increased precipitation 
chances to the eastern portions of the forecast area.
 
Uncertainty remains on the track and timing of the low pressure 
system, but recent guidance has it tracking north towards the 
Northeast away from the Mid-Atlantic, possibly making a cyclonic
loop near Long Island. The most likely impact from the nearby 
system will be increased winds due to the tight pressure 
gradient overhead. North/northwest winds blow around 15-20 mph 
Friday and Saturday before decreasing Sunday and into the workweek.

In addition to mainly dry conditions and gusty winds, 
temperatures gradually warm each day. On Friday, highs will be 
in the 60s for most (50s mtns) with overnight lows dipping into 
the 40s and 50s. By the end of the weekend, high temperatures 
will be in the 70s for most (60s mtns) with most staying in the 
50s overnight.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Ceilings will vary between MVFR and VFR into this evening before
dropping more readily to IFR. An area of rain showers will move
across through about 22Z, with embedded TSRA near KCHO.

Guidance is in better agreement that ceilings will lower to IFR
tonight as showers increase in coverage across the area. IFR 
ceilings and on and off showers then continue through the day 
Wednesday. Winds will be out of the northeast through Wednesday,
and should gust to around 15-25 knots on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Northeast winds on Thursday shift to north/northwesterly on Friday, 
gusting 15 to 20 knots each afternoon. On Friday, metro terminals 
gust 20 to 25 knots. VFR conditions are expected both days under
dry conditions.

&&

.MARINE...
East to northeast winds increase through mid week, with gales
possibly mainly around southern Maryland Wednesday into
Thursday. Periods of rain are also expected, which will reduce
visibility. Persistent onshore flow may result in waves as high
as 3 to 6 feet in the wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay off
southern Maryland by mid week.

Northeast winds on Thursday blow 15 to 25 knots over the waters with 
gusts up to 35 knots possible. A Gale Watch is in effect until 
Thursday afternoon for the middle portions of the Chesapeake 
Bay off southern Maryland. On Friday, north/northwest winds 
blow 20 to 30 knots over the waters with gusts up to 35 knots 
possible. Gale conditions are possible over the southern 
portions of the waters with additional watches possible.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Tides are expected to snap back to the north, with anomalies 
rapidly rising again later tonight through the day Tuesday. 
Elevated tide levels are then expected through much of the week 
as a strong area of high pressure builds to our north, leading 
to persistent onshore flow. The wind direction will be closer to
northeasterly rather than easterly, so the tidal levels are 
expected to increase with southward extent in the Chesapeake 
Bay. Many locations will likely reach Minor Flood Stage on 
Tuesday and Wednesday, and Annapolis could come close to 
flooding tonight as well. Moderate flooding can't be ruled out 
at some locations, especially at Annapolis by mid week. A 
coastal low is expected to develop offshore later this week, 
potentially prolonging coastal flood concerns.

&&
